label: def:quantum-universe
title: Quantum Universe
html:
Definition. A quantum universe is a tuple (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) consisting of:

  1. an R-linear braided monoidal category \mathbf{C} over a commutative ring R, whose unit endomorphisms recover the ground ring: R \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{End}_{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{1}), r \mapsto r \cdot \mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{1}},
  2. a distinguished object A \in \mathrm{Ob}(\mathbf{C}) equipped with a Frobenius–Hopf algebra structure,
  3. an R-linear faithful fibre functor \tau \colon \mathbf{C} \to R\text{-}\mathbf{Mod},

satisfying the following four axioms:

  1. (Temporal braiding) The ordering \prec_c induced by the braiding c_{V,W} \colon V \otimes W \xrightarrow{\sim} W \otimes V on the Hecke basis of A is well-founded.
  2. (Frobenius--Hopf) A carries compatible associative multiplication \mu, co-multiplication \Delta, unit \eta, co-unit \varepsilon, and antipode S. The space A acts on every V \in \mathbf{C} via a categorical representation \rho_V \colon A \otimes V \to V.
  3. (Symmetric Frobenius) The left and right categorical traces on \mathrm{End}(A) coincide. These traces are defined by the self-duality of A, which the snake identities for the pairing \int_A \circ\, \mu supply in axiom 2.
  4. (Wedderburn semisimplicity) A is semisimple, with a finite index set \widehat{A} of blocks. Each block \lambda \in \widehat{A} carries a central idempotent p_\lambda, and these
\begin{aligned}
\text{do not mix:} && p_\lambda \circ p_\mu &= 0 && (\lambda \neq \mu), \\
\text{and span:}   && \textstyle\sum_{\lambda \in \widehat{A}} p_\lambda &= \mathrm{id}_A. &&
\end{aligned}

Each block further carries a Frobenius weight \int_A p_\lambda invertible in R, and a quantum dimension \dim_q(\lambda) invertible in R.

Rigidity of \mathbf{C} is not required here. It is imposed on a quantum observable universe, where duals carry the antiparticles.

On the ground ring. R is a commutative ring, not a field, and "invertible in R" in axiom 4 is strictly stronger than "nonzero" once R has non-units. The two clauses coincide only over a field.

On the substrate parameter. The axioms ask of R only that it be a commutative ring. The substrate parameter is emergent rather than carried: no q appears among the data, the balancing twist determines it on the defining representation, and it lands in \mathrm{End}(\mathbf{1}) \cong R. The construction runs R, then the R-linear braided category, then the twist supplied by the tensor and braiding, and q is read from that twist. The invertibility in axiom 4 is quantified over this universe's own blocks, so it constrains the pair (R, \mathbf{C}) and not R alone. A ring therefore limits which decompositions it can carry rather than being admissible or not.

That limit is real. In \mathbb{Z}[q, q^{-1}] the units are exactly \pm q^{k}, while each quantum integer is a monomial times a cyclotomic product of positive degree — [2]_q = q^{-1}\Phi_4(q), [3]_q = q^{-2}\Phi_3\Phi_6, [4]_q = q^{-3}\Phi_4\Phi_8. No [m]_q with m \geq 2 is a unit there, so over that ring the block index collapses to the trivial block: the axioms are satisfiable, but only degenerately, and none of the framework's Hecke decompositions fit. Inverting the cyclotomics is what makes a non-degenerate universe available:

  R \;=\; \mathbb{Z}[q, q^{-1}]\bigl[\, \Phi_d(q)^{-1} \;:\; d \geq 2 \,\bigr],

whose spectrum is the q-line with the roots of unity of order \geq 2 removed. Starting at d = 1 would additionally delete q = 1, which the classical limit needs, and nothing requires it: q^{n} - 1 = (q-1)\,[n]_q, so q^n - 1 is a unit exactly when q - 1 is, and the constructs inverting q - 1 live past the archimedean wall.

This is a choice of instance, not a strengthening of the definition. The property that q and every \Phi_d(q), d \geq 2, are invertible — QOU.AlgebraicSubstrate.IsQGeneric — belongs to the construction of a Hecke-type universe, where it is what discharges the axiom-4 fields. It is deliberately not a hypothesis of def:quantum-universe, which stays at CommRing. The ring above is the initial object satisfying the property, so any other base with it — \mathbb{Q}(q), a real algebra at the substrate anchor, a neighbouring convention's Laurent ring — receives a unique map from it and inherits the construction. The map runs outward; no universe is asked to embed in this ring, and injectivity is never required — the evaluation at q = 1 is not injective, and must not be.

The identification R \cong \mathrm{End}_{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{1}) in item 1 is a genuine hypothesis and not a consequence of R-linearity. Linearity supplies only the ring map r \mapsto r \cdot \mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{1}}; its bijectivity is the statement that \mathbf{1} is simple, and it is what licenses reading the block data \int_A p_\lambda and \dim_q(\lambda) as elements of R rather than as endomorphisms of the unit. It is stated here because the rest of the paper uses it silently — for instance in taking the substrate parameter q \in \mathrm{End}(\mathbf{1}).
